paper_title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The growing diversity of large language models (LLMs) has motivated LLM routing as paradigm for leveraging complementary capabilities, where different models are selected and coordinated according to their strengths, costs, and suitability for each query (Chen et al., 2024a; Ding et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025). Depending on how model calls are organized, current routing approaches generally follow three paradigms: single-round routing selects single model for one-shot execution (Chen et al., 2024b; Feng et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026), multi-round routing makes successive model selections conditioned on intermediate outputs (Zhang et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2026), and agentic routing organizes multiple models into structured collaborative workflows (Yue et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026b). Although routing decisions within each paradigm can adapt to the query, the execution paradigm itself is typically fixed in advance. As result, the router can adapt which models to use, but not how model calls should be organized for different queries. This raises natural question: how can we unify these routing paradigms within single policy that jointly adapts execution mode and model selection to each query? Unifying these routing paradigms within single policy is non-trivial. Single-round, multi-round, and agentic routing follow different execution structures and decision processes, requiring common formulation that accommodates all three while preserving their distinct behaviors. sections.title: RouteWeaver
sections.content: this structural challenge, two learning problems are particularly important. First, different queries may favor different execution modes, yet determining which mode is appropriate requires reasoning about the task before its execution unfolds. unified router must therefore learn when single-round, multi-round, or agentic execution is most suitable for each query. Second, selecting an appropriate mode alone is insufficient, since each mode demands different form of model selection and coordination. Single-round routing requires choosing an effective model directly, multi-round routing must adapt subsequent selections to intermediate outputs, and agentic routing additionally organizes models through roles and dependencies. The router must therefore learn not only which mode to use, but also how to execute effectively within the selected mode. To address these challenges, we propose RouteWeaver, unified routing policy that learns to select among single-round, multi-round, and agentic execution paradigms and perform model selection within the chosen paradigm. We first introduce unified routing format that expresses all three paradigms through common action grammar for mode selection and subsequent routing decisions. To jointly optimize these two levels of decisions, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, allowing the router to first learn how to execute within each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver on benchmarks spanning mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves 61.4% average accuracy, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines across the five domains. We further study performancecost trade-offs and generalization on held-out benchmarks (AIME, GPQA-D, and BBH). With α = 0.1, Worker inference cost decreases by 23% with only 1.0-point accuracy drop, while RouteWeaver achieves 53.7% average accuracy on held-out benchmarks, an 18.28% relative improvement over the strongest baseline. Ablations and routing analyses further validate COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration and reveal adaptive execution choices across tasks. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate unified LLM routing across single-round, multi-round, and agentic execution paradigms, enabling single policy to adapt both the execution mode and model selection to each query rather than committing to predefined routing schema. We propose RouteWeaver, featuring COMET-GRPO, which decouples credit assignment for mode selection and within-mode execution, together with progressive exploration that gradually transitions the router from learning how to execute each mode to autonomously deciding when to use it for different queries. Extensive experiments across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall demonstrate the effectiveness of unified routing over existing routers and fixedmode strategies. Further analyses examine performancecost trade-offs, routing behavior, and the contributions of the proposed training components.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 EXECUTION PARADIGMS FOR LLM ROUTING Existing LLM routing methods can be categorized by how model calls are organized. (1) Singleround routing selects one model for each query, typically based on model capability, query difficulty, or performancecost trade-offs. RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2025) learns routing from preference data, while RouterDC (Chen et al., 2024b) and GraphRouter (Feng et al., 2025b) model query model relations. ICL-Router (Wang et al., 2026) further improves routing through learned model (2) Multi-round routing allows routing decisions to evolve across calls using representations. intermediate outputs. Router-R1 (Zhang et al., 2025) formulates routing as sequential decision process with repeated model selection and response aggregation, while R2-Reasoner (Shao et al., 2026) combines task decomposition with model allocation for intermediate reasoning. (3) Agentic routing organizes multiple models into collaborative workflows. MasRouter (Yue et al., 2025) jointly considers collaboration structures, agent roles, and model choices, while GraphPlanner (Feng

Top right, multi-round: the router selects Workers sequentially using accumulated observations. Bottom, agentic: the router selects Workers, assigns roles, and specifies dependencies between calls; the depicted workflow is illustrative, and its roles and dependencies vary across queries. et al., 2026b) generates query-dependent workflows with modelrole assignments and explicit interactions. Despite adaptive routing within each paradigm, prior approaches fix the execution paradigm in advance. In contrast, RouteWeaver unifies single-round, multi-round, and agentic routing as selectable modes of one policy, jointly learning mode selection and within-mode execution. 2.2 REINFORCEMENT LEARNING FOR AGENTIC LLMS Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central approach for improving the reasoning and interactive capabilities of LLMs. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) replaces critic-based advantage estimation with group-relative rewards and has inspired several variants. Dr.GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) addresses optimization biases in GRPO, while DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) improves training stability through asymmetric clipping and dynamic sampling. GDPO (Liu et al., 2026) further decouples reward normalization for multi-reward optimization. RL has also been extended to interactive agents. Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) and ReTool (Feng et al., 2026a) train LLMs to interleave reasoning with search or tool interactions, while GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025a) introduces episodeand step-level relative advantages for finer credit assignment in multi-turn agents. Building on these advances, COMET-GRPO adapts group-relative optimization to unified LLM routing, where mode selection and within-mode execution form two coupled decision levels and receive separate credit signals.

sections.title: 4 RO U T EWE A V E R
sections.content: Building on the above formulation, RouteWeaver unifies single-round, multi-round, and agentic routing in one policy. This raises three challenges. First, their heterogeneous execution structures require common representation. Second, performance depends jointly on mode selection and withinmode execution, calling for differentiated learning signals. Third, mode selection requires sufficient experience across modes to avoid early bias. RouteWeaver addresses these challenges through unified routing formulation (Section 4.1), COMET-GRPO for coordinated modeexecution learning (Section 4.2), and progressive exploration toward autonomous routing (Section 4.3). Figure 2: Overview of RouteWeaver. (a) One routing policy πθ selects an execution mode, then calls frozen Workers;Multi-round calls automatically use the latest observation, while agentic calls include role assignments and router-selected references to earlier outputs.Returned observations are appended to its context until it emits the final answer. (b) COMET-GRPO computes mode-level and within-mode advantages per reward component, mixes them (Eq. (7)), and assigns Amode to mode-selection tokens and Ainner to subsequent router tokens. (c) Progressive training moves mode selection from assigned modes to the router in three stages. 4.1 UNIFIED TRAJECTORY REPRESENTATION AND EXECUTION To this end, we represent each routing process as mode-conditioned trajectory. Given query x, the router first selects an execution mode πθ( x), = {single, multi, agentic}, and subsequently generates routing actions conditioned on the query and the accumulated interaction context. Each Worker call specifies Worker and sub-query s; agentic calls additionally specify role and references to completed calls. Multi-round execution passes the previous observation to each subsequent call, while agentic execution passes the referenced outputs to role-structured and potentially parallel calls. Single-round execution contains exactly one Worker call. The serialization format and mode-specific constraints are detailed in Appendix A.1. Executing an action returns the Worker outputs as an observation ot, which is appended to the router context before the next decision. sections.title: 4.2 COMET-GRPO
sections.content: Joint mode selection and execution create an ambiguous credit-assignment problem. low-reward trajectory may result from selecting an unsuitable execution mode, from executing an otherwise suitable mode poorly, or from both. Standard GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) does not distinguish these cases: it assigns the same trajectory-level relative advantage to the mode-selection tokens and all subsequent router-generated tokens. We therefore decompose relative feedback into two complementary comparisons: an across-mode comparison for mode selection and within-mode comparison for execution conditioned on the selected mode. COMET-GRPO (COordinated ModeExecution Training) uses these two signals to optimize the two decision levels separately within shared policy. Two levels of relative advantage. In free group, each rollout selects its own mode, so the group need not cover all modes. Let Vm contain the retained rollouts that selected m, with mean µm of the same component. For rollout with mode mi, Amode = µmi µ σ + ϵ , Ainner = ri µmi σ + ϵ . sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate RouteWeaver across five task domains to examine whether jointly selecting and executing different routing modes improves over methods restricted to fixed execution paradigm. We further study its performancecost trade-off, isolate the contributions of COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration, and analyze how execution-mode choices vary across tasks. Additional dataset, evaluation, and implementation details are provided in the appendices.

sections.title: 5.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Datasets. Our evaluation comprises nine benchmarks spanning five domains: Math, MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) and Omni-MATH (Gao et al., 2025); Code, APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), and TACO (Li et al., 2023); Knowledge, SuperGPQA (Du et al., 2025); Reason, SATBench (Wei et al., 2025); and Recall, TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) and SimpleQA-Verified (Haas et al., 2025). Test questions do not overlap with the training questions used for router optimization. Dataset composition, training pools, and evaluation sets are provided in Appendix B.1. Router and Worker models. The router is Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025) with all parameters fine-tuned. The Worker pool contains six frozen models: Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30BA3B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Llama Team, AI @ Meta, 2024), Gemma-3-27B-IT (Gemma Team, 2025), and Gemini-2.5-FlashLite (Gemini Team, Google, 2025). The router refers to Workers only by anonymous IDs with capability descriptions and never sees model names or prices. Model identifiers and serving providers are listed in Appendix B.3. Baselines. We compare RouteWeaver with ten routers spanning all three execution paradigms. Single-round baselines include Router-KNN and Router-MLP (Hu et al., 2024), RouterDC (Chen et al., 2024b), and GraphRouter (Feng et al., 2025b); multi-round baselines include Prompt LLM and Router-KNN-MR following Zhang et al. (2025), R2-Reasoner (Shao et al., 2026), and RouterR1 (Zhang et al., 2025); and agentic baselines include MasRouter (Yue et al., 2025) and GraphPlanner (Feng et al., 2026b). 5.2 PERFORMANCE ACROSS EXECUTION PARADIGMS RouteWeaver substantially outperforms fixed-paradigm routers. Table 1 compares RouteWeaver with single-round, multi-round, and agentic routing baselines across the five evaluation domains. RouteWeaver reaches an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline (55.3%, Router-R1). Its relative improvements over the strongest single-round, multi-round, and agentic baselines are 26.08%, 11.03%, and 31.20%, respectively, and it leads all baselines in each of the five domains. Adaptive execution provides broad but task-dependent gains. RouteWeaver leads the strongest baseline in every evaluation domain, with relative improvements ranging from 5.20% on Recall to 12.52% on Math. Importantly, the strongest fixed-paradigm baseline varies across domains: multi-round routers perform best among the baselines on Math, Code, and Knowledge, whereas single-round routers are strongest on Reason and Recall. This variation suggests that no single execution paradigm is uniformly preferable across tasks, motivating RouteWeavers queryadaptive mode selection. Section 5.5 further examines how RouteWeaver distributes queries across execution modes. 5.3 PERFORMANCECOST TRADE-OFF Efficiency preferences allow RouteWeaver to operate at different accuracycost points. Figure 4 reveals strongly task-dependent execution preferences. Math uses all three modes, with 19% of queries routed to single-round, 50% to multi-round, and 31% to agentic execution. Code is dominated by multi-round routing (84%), whereas Knowledge primarily uses single-round execution (72%). The contrast is strongest for Reason and Recall: 99% of reasoning queries are routed to agentic execution, while 96% of recall queries use single-round routing. These results reveal substantially different execution-mode preferences across task domains. Figure 4: Share of selected execution modes across evaluation domains for RouteWeaver (α = 0). Each bar shows the proportion of test queries routed to single-round, multi-round, and agentic execution. Generalization to held-out benchmarks. To evaluate whether the learned routing policy transfers beyond the datasets used for router training, we further test RouteWeaver on AIME (AI-MO, 2024; Zhang & Math-AI Team, 2025) for Math, GPQA-Diamond (GPQA-D) (Rein et al., 2024) for Knowledge, and BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023) for Reason. We compare against one representative baseline from each execution paradigm  (Table 3)  . RouteWeaver achieves the best accuracy on all three held-out benchmarks, reaching an average of 53.7%, an 18.28% relative improvement over Router-R1 (45.4%). The gains are consistent across all three benchmarks, with improvements of 11.4, 7.1, and 6.4 points over Router-R1 on AIME, GPQA-D, and BBH, respectively. The learned execution behavior also varies across held-out benchmarks, with agentic execution accounting for 75% of AIME queries but only 12% of BBH queries. These results indicate that RouteWeavers adaptive routing behavior extends to unseen benchmarks within the same task domains. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented RouteWeaver, unified LLM routing framework that treats the execution paradigm itself as routing decision, jointly learning mode selection and within-mode execution. By combining COMET-GRPO with progressive exploration, RouteWeaver learns when to use single-round, multi-round, or agentic execution and how to route effectively within the selected mode. Across five task domains, RouteWeaver consistently outperforms fixed-paradigm routing baselines, exhibits task-dependent execution preferences, and supports different performancecost operating points. These results suggest that effective LLM routing should adapt not only which models to invoke, but also how their computation is organized. Extending this unified perspective to richer execution structures and tool-augmented environments is an interesting direction for future work.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with implementation and debugging, drafting and editing portions of the manuscript for clarity, and surveying and summarizing relevant literature. All AI-assisted code and manuscript content were reviewed by the authors, and AI-assisted code was inspected and tested before use. The authors take full responsibility for the final content, claims, and artifacts presented in this work. ETHICS STATEMENT This work studies routing among existing language models using established benchmarks and does not involve human-subject experiments or the collection of private user data. RouteWeaver inherits the limitations and potential harms of its underlying Worker models, including biased, unsafe, or factually incorrect outputs, which may propagate across multiple model calls. Our experiments are intended to evaluate routing methodology rather than safety-critical deployment. Practical deployments should therefore apply appropriate model-level safety mechanisms and comply with the licenses and usage policies of the underlying models and datasets. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT We provide the complete formulation and training objectives of RouteWeaver in Section 4, and describe the datasets, router and Worker models, and baselines in Section 5.1. The appendices further document the routing serialization and execution constraints (Appendix A.1), dataset construction and evaluation sets (Appendix B.1), task-specific evaluation procedures (Appendix B.2), model and serving configurations (Appendix B.3), reward and cost definitions (Appendix C.1), optimization details (Appendix C.2), and training hyperparameters, decoding settings, and call budgets (Appendix C.3). Together, these sections document the training and evaluation setup used for RouteWeaver. Code is available at https://github.com/LaughKing/RouteWeaver. REFERENCES AI-MO. sections.title: A ROUTING INTERFACE
sections.content: A.1 ACTION FORMAT The routers output is written with the four elements illustrated in Table 4: one mode element, followed by route elements interleaved with environment-inserted observation elements, and final answer element. Workers are named by their anonymous IDs. Table 4: Schematic of the shared trajectory representation. Element Illustrative form Mode selection <mode>agentic</mode> Worker call <route model="worker 2" role="verifier" refs="n1"> Check the proposed solution.</route> Returned output <observation id="n2">...</observation> Final response <answer>...</answer> Produced by Router Router Environment Router Each Worker receives the sub-query written in its route element together with the mode-specific context described below. trajectory must follow the grammar and the execution constraints of its mode: Single-round: exactly one call <route model="w">s</route>, followed by the final answer. Multi-round: two to four sequential calls of the same form, one per router turn; each call after the first also receives the previous observation. Agentic: calls of the form <route model="w" role="r" refs="P ">s</route>, with {planner, executor, verifier, summarizer} and comma-separated list of node IDs (empty for the first layer). Several routes in one router turn form layer and run in parallel; route may reference only outputs of earlier layers, which the environment inserts into that Workers input. Each output returns as <observation id="nk" role="r">. At most eight Worker calls and ten router action turns are allowed. The first action that violates the grammar or an execution constraint of the mode terminates the trajectory with rewards (1, 1) (Appendix C.1). A.2 EXAMPLE TRAJECTORIES Figure 5 shows one abbreviated trajectory per mode from the evaluation of the reported router.

sections.title: B EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: B.1 DATASETS Training data. The router is trained on 3,200 queries from seven datasets  (Table 5)  . Each training batch contains 32 queries with fixed domain quotas: 7 Math, 7 Code (4 APPS and 3 LiveCodeBench), 6 Knowledge, 7 Reason, and 5 Recall. Evaluation data. Evaluation uses 1,060 test questions that do not overlap with the training questions: 120 each from MATH, Omni-MATH, APPS, LiveCodeBench, SuperGPQA, SATBench, TriviaQA, and SimpleQA-Verified, and 100 from TACO.

sections.title: RouteWeaver
sections.content: Table 5: Training data by domain. Domain Dataset #Queries Per batch Math Code Knowledge Reason Recall Total Omni-MATH APPS, LiveCodeBench SuperGPQA SATBench TriviaQA, PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023) 700 400, 300 600 700 200, 300 3,200 7 4, 3 6 7 5 B.2 EVALUATION PROTOCOL Per-dataset scoring. Every question receives binary score, and we report accuracy per dataset. MATH, Omni-MATH: symbolic mathematical equivalence with the reference answer. APPS: the extracted program is executed in sandbox on standard input and is correct if its output matches on all test cases. LiveCodeBench, TACO: extracted code is executed and is correct if it passes all retained test cases. At most 40 test cases are kept per problem; for LiveCodeBench, test cases are additionally kept in their original order only while their cumulative serialized size stays within 256 KB (at least one is always kept). Both rules are deterministic, so the full official test suites are not always used. SuperGPQA: the last option letter in the response must match the reference exactly. SATBench: the last occurrence of SAT or UNSAT in the response must match the reference label. SimpleQA-Verified: normalized exact match, or the reference answer appears in the response as whole-word match. TriviaQA: exact match with any reference alias after SQuAD-style normalization (lowercasing and removing punctuation, articles, and extra whitespace). Aggregation. Domain accuracy is the unweighted mean of the accuracies of its constituent datasets, and Avg is the unweighted mean of the five domain accuracies. B.3 ROUTER AND WORKER MODELS Router. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, with full-parameter fine-tuning. The KL reference policy is the frozen initial router. Only the router is trained. Workers. The six Workers are frozen and are exposed to the router under fixed anonymous IDs. The routers system prompt lists each ID with fixed capability description  (Table 6)  and never contains model names or prices. worker 1 and worker 2 are deployed locally on two NVIDIA A100 GPUs, and worker 3 to worker 6 are accessed through OpenRouter; the serving setup is the same in training and evaluation.

sections.title: C TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: C.1 REWARDS AND COST ACCOUNTING This section completes the definitions of Section 4. Rewards and excluded rollouts. Each trajectory receives the two rewards of Eq. 5. Correctness is judged by the dataset-specific scorers of Appendix B.2. The first action that violates the grammar or an execution constraint of the mode (Appendix A.1) terminates the trajectory, which receives (1, 1), remains in V, and enters the group statistics like any other rollout. rollout affected by an infrastructure failure, such as Worker call returning no response, is not attributed to the router

When the efficiency reward is enabled (α > 0), trajectories with incomplete cost records are excluded from in the same way, so they enter neither reward component nor the corresponding updates. Cost measure. C(τ ) sums the inference cost of every Worker call in τ , computed from the calls input and output tokens at the fixed reference prices of Table 7 (in USD per million tokens). The mode and inner advantages supervise disjoint token sets with separate normalization. i,c = AGRPO i,c + Ainner i,c C.3 HYPERPARAMETERS AND DECODING Training. We use batch size of 32 queries, 8 rollouts per query, learning rate of 106, KL coefficient of 0.001 against the frozen initial router, and zero entropy regularization. Each run, for α {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5}, starts independently from the same initial router at step 0, is trained for 90 steps, and is evaluated at its final checkpoint. Steps 125 form the cold-start phase: forced modes, standard GRPO on the task reward with the standard-deviation gate, global token reduction, and no support term. After step 25 each run continues its own training trajectory, enabling the mode/inner decomposition and segment-wise reduction and mixing the task and efficiency advantages with its fixed α; the KL reference remains the frozen initial router. The forced ratio ρb decreases linearly from 1 at data batch index 25 to 0 at batch index 75, and the support coefficient is 0.002 ρb. The support floor is δ = 0.05 with λ0 = 0.002, the clipping ranges are η = η+ = 0.2, and dual clipping uses = 3. The optimizer is AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.999), ϵ = 108, and weight decay 0.01, using constant learning rate without warmup or decay and global gradient-norm clipping at 1.0. Each step performs single on-policy update over all 32 8 = 256 trajectories of the batch, so πold is the policy that generated them. In the ablation without progressive exploration, ρb = 0 for all b, so the support term (λb = λ0ρb) is inactive as well. Decoding. Router, training: temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95, top-k disabled. Router, testing: greedy decoding. Workers, training and testing: temperature 0.2, at most 4,096 output tokens; top-p and top-k are not set and follow provider defaults. Worker requests carry fixed seed (42), which providers may ignore, and disable thinking/reasoning modes. Because Workers sample, systemlevel evaluation is not fully deterministic. Each evaluation question receives one system rollout. Call budgets and lengths. Identical in training and evaluation. Single-round: exactly one Worker call. Multi-round: two to four sequential calls. Agentic: at most eight Worker calls and at most ten router action turns. Prompts are limited to 6,144 tokens, the multi-turn response budget to 12,288 tokens, the mode-declaration turn to 64 tokens, and each observation to 2,048 tokens.
